title: Press release
draft: The IMF Executive Board completed the third review under the Republic of Congo's SDR 324 million Extended Credit Facility, approving an immediate disbursement of SDR 32.4 million (about US$43 million), bringing total disbursements to SDR 226.8 million. Although three out of five performance criteria were missed, strong corrective actions were taken. The IMF recommends sustained structural reform implementation, fiscal consolidation via reducing oil-related subsidies, and strengthened public financial and debt management to ensure debt sustainability and support resilient, inclusive growth.

title: Executive summary
draft: Congo's economic recovery faces declining oil prices and high public debt, which remains sustainable but "in distress". Under the three-year Extended Credit Facility arrangement of SDR 324 million (200 percent of quota), program performance was weak: three out of five performance criteria, two out of five indicative targets, and three out of five structural benchmarks were missed. Economic recovery and debt reduction require regaining fiscal space through strong corrective actions, including rationalizing public expenditures and reducing fuel subsidies by increasing gasoline fuel prices by 25 percent.

title: Context
draft: Congo needs economic diversification to address fragilities, yet fiscal space is constrained by high debt and reduced oil revenues, which are typically 2½ times non-oil revenues. The main judgement is that the government must reconcile immediate cost-of-living priorities with fiscal discipline. Following expanded subsidies in 2022, fiscal consolidation is critical for 2023 to put the deficit and public debt firmly on a downward path. Authorities should reduce untargeted fuel price subsidies, implement carefully costed targeted social assistance, and maintain sizeable fiscal efforts over the medium term.

title: Recent Economic Developments, Outlook, And Risks
draft: In 2022, economic growth reached 1.7 percent, driven by 3.3 percent non-oil growth, while oil production contracted by 3.8 percent and inflation averaged 3.0 percent. The current account surplus reached 19.4 percent of GDP. For 2023, real GDP growth is projected to rise to 4 percent and inflation is expected to average 3.5 percent. Crucially, the economic outlook is predicated on progress in structural and governance reforms to support economic diversification away from oil, while risks remain tilted to the downside.

title: Program Performance
draft: Two end-2022 performance criteria were missed, including the adjusted basic non-oil primary balance target by 0.3 percent of non-oil GDP, and the continuous criterion on non-accumulation of external arrears was breached. Furthermore, implementation of structural reforms has been weak, as only two structural benchmarks were implemented. The authorities request waivers of non-observance based on corrective actions that support offsetting fiscal consolidation, including a prior action on fuel price adjustment, and have committed to continue work on missed benchmarks to ensure their completion.

title: Policy Discussions: A. Fiscal Policy
draft: IMF staff recommend that fiscal policy support growth while safeguarding debt sustainability through medium-term consolidation and expenditure reprioritization. To compensate for 2022 slippages, the 2023 budget targets a non-oil primary deficit of 11.8 percent of non-oil GDP, reflecting a 3.9 percentage point consolidation relative to 2022. Underpinned by phased fuel subsidy removals and revenue mobilization, consolidation is projected to reduce public debt from 92.5 to 72.3 percent of GDP between 2022 and 2028. Debt is assessed as sustainable, though classified in distress.

title: B. Public Investment and Debt Management
draft: Debt reduction progress is weakened by newly recognized domestic arrears. Although authorities repaid CFAF 431 billion (5 percent of GDP) in 2022, they recognized CFAF 360 billion (4 percent of GDP) in new domestic social arrears, while another CFAF 240 billion is being audited. Staff recommend establishing a multi-year domestic arrears payment plan, restructuring the debt management office to enhance coordination and transparency, and reforming public investment management by formalizing standard project assessment and selection criteria that integrate climate dimensions and risk analysis.

title: C. Governance, Transparency, and Broader Structural Reforms
draft: Momentum in governance and transparency reforms remains critical for program success. The authorities expect four out of five remaining SIGFIP modules to be ready by end-June 2024, and all five operational by end-2024. A convention transferring oil export revenues to the single treasury account is expected by mid-2023. Further key commitments include submitting conflict-of-interest declarations by end-April 2024, finalizing an action plan for end-January 2024, and establishing EITI-compliant cadasters by end-June 2024. Broadening access to finance and strengthening financial sector resilience should also continue.

title: Program Modalities And Other Issues
draft: The program is fully financed for the next 12 months, and authorities requested waivers for missed performance criteria backed by corrective fiscal consolidation measures. The section's main judgement is that Congo's capacity to repay the Fund is assessed to be adequate but subject to significant risks. Under the baseline, total Fund credit outstanding peaks at 220 percent of quota (SDR 356.4 million, 3.2 percent of GDP) in 2024, while debt service to the Fund peaks at 0.5 percent of GDP in 2029.

title: Staff Appraisal
draft: Congo must balance fiscal consolidation with growth and poverty reduction after new subsidies widened the 2022 non-oil primary deficit by an additional 0.8 percent of non-oil GDP. Gradually removing fuel price subsidies yields 4.2 percent of non-oil GDP over 2023–25 to restore sustainability, while domestic arrears reached 4.2 percent of GDP. Although three performance criteria were missed over the past 6 months, strong corrective actions demonstrate commitment. Therefore, staff supports the completion of the third review under the ECF arrangement and requested waivers.

title: Figures and statistical tables
draft: While real GDP growth is projected to recover to 4.0 percent in 2023 and total public debt declines from 92.5 percent of GDP in 2022 to 72.3 percent in 2028, lower oil prices reduce oil revenues. To improve transparency and governance and protect public resources, key recommendations call for increasing gasoline fuel prices by at least 10 percent, rationalizing transfers to inefficient SOEs to yield 4.4 percent of non-oil GDP, enacting hydrocarbon-related VAT reforms, and expanding social assistance to protect vulnerable households.

title: Annex I. Country engagement strategy
draft: To overcome fragility rooted in oil dependence, with oil generating 80 percent of exports and almost two thirds of fiscal revenues, and poverty affecting around 40 percent of the population, Congo must diversify its economy, strengthen institutions, and preserve macroeconomic stability. The report recommends pursuing deep governance and structural reforms guided by the National Development Plan 2022–26 and supported by the ECF arrangement (200 percent of quota, SDR 324.0 million). Achieving these goals requires addressing capacity constraints, securing partner financing, and sustaining program ownership.

title: Annex II. Risk assessment matrix
draft: The Risk Assessment Matrix assesses baseline risks categorized by probabilities: low indicates below 10 percent, medium between 10 and 30 percent, and high between 30 and 50 percent, with conjunctural shocks spanning 12 to 18 months. Significant risks include regional conflict escalation, commodity price volatility, and global slowdowns. The matrix's central recommendation is to continue fiscal and structural reforms, employ oil revenues to build fiscal buffers, accelerate non-oil revenue mobilization, streamline non-priority spending, and strengthen targeted social safety nets to reduce vulnerabilities and debt pressures.

title: Appendix I. Letter of intent
draft: Under the ECF arrangement, program performance was mixed: two of the five quantitative performance criteria were not met at end-December 2022 and one was not met at end-March 2023, while structural benchmarks experienced delays. In response, the authorities committed to corrective measures, including fuel price increases and expected SNPC dividends of at least CFAF 10 billion (0.2 percent of non-oil GDP). Consequently, the authorities request waivers of non-observance, target modifications, and completion of the third review to enable a disbursement of SDR 32.4 million.

title: Attachment I. Memorandum of economic and financial policies
draft: Economic growth reached 1.7 percent in 2022 and is projected to rise to 4.0 percent in 2023. The memorandum recommends gradual fiscal consolidation while safeguarding debt sustainability and social spending. Authorities commit to reducing the non-oil primary deficit from 15.7 to 5.5 percent of non-oil GDP over 2022–28, helping lower public debt from 98 percent of GDP in 2023 to 72.3 percent by 2028. Key measures include phasing out fuel subsidies, settling CFAF 110 billion of domestic arrears in 2023, and strengthening governance, transparency, and public investment.

title: Attachment II. Technical memorandum of understanding
draft: This Technical Memorandum of Understanding specifies criteria, adjusters, and reporting requirements for monitoring Congo's Extended Credit Facility arrangement. It defines program targets, treating external debt as concessional when its grant element reaches at least 35 percent, discounted at 5 percent. Crucially, the framework mandates that new pre-financing backed by future natural resource deliveries is strictly prohibited under the program. It requires the authorities to consult IMF staff prior to entering any new non-CFA Franc debt commitments and report quarterly monitoring assessments within 45 days.

title: Debt sustainability analysis
draft: The Republic of Congo’s overall and external debt are classified as "in distress", but debt is assessed as "sustainable". Total public debt declined to 92.5 percent of GDP at end-2022. Under the baseline, the external debt service-to-revenue ratio falls from 29 percent in 2023 below the 14 percent threshold by 2026, though the PV of public debt-to-GDP breaches the 35 percent benchmark through 2033. The main recommendation is for authorities to pursue fiscal consolidation, enact policies for diversification, clear domestic arrears, and enhance debt management.

title: Staff supplement
draft: The authorities met the two prior actions under the third review of the Extended Credit Facility arrangement, leaving the thrust of the Staff Appraisal unchanged. A joint ministerial decree announced a 24 percent increase in the price of gasoline effective July 15, 2023, broadly in line with the 25 percent price increase initially reflected in budget projections. Additionally, a ministerial instruction established legal provisions for depositing fees collected as part of the retail price formula into an on-budget, transparent and monitorable account.

title: Executive Director's statement
draft: Despite mixed program performance caused by external shocks, which led to missing two quantitative performance criteria at end-December 2022, Congolese authorities took decisive corrective actions. Economic growth revised to 1.7 percent in 2022 is projected to rebound to 4 percent in 2023, while gasoline prices were increased by 30 percent in 2023 to reverse overruns. Reaffirming their reform commitment and projected non-oil primary balance improvement of nearly 5 percentage points of GDP, the authorities request the completion of the third review under the ECF-supported program.
